claims.wording: Historians of the silver trade generally explain the Manila trade by China's demand for silver. Silver was worth more in Ming China than anywhere else. Spanish America produced it at low cost. From 1571 Manila gave the two a direct meeting place. Flynn and Giráldez (1995), Atwell (1982) and von Glahn (1996) all explain it this way.
claims.notes:
Quote: "it was the elevated value of silver inside China that created the opportunities for profit around the globe" (Flynn and Giráldez 1995, p. 206); "Manila was the crucial entrepôt linking substantial, direct, and continuous trade between America and Asia for the first time in history." (Flynn and Giráldez 1995, p. 201); "Silver poured into China because the Chinese market valued it more highly than anywhere else in the world" (von Glahn, *Fountain of Fortune*, ch. 4, p. 133); "foreign traders found the Chinese demand for silver almost insatiable" (Atwell 1982, p. 79)
Page image: web entry, no page scan (JSTOR PDF and book chapter; check: Read)
Field: this is the view of world historians and historians of Chinese money.

confidence.rationale: high that these three say this. It is an interpretation.

claims.independenceNote: Three Sources, all later scholarship, and not independent of each other. Flynn and Giráldez (1995, p. 206) name Atwell as the main earlier voice.

supports.citation: Dennis O. Flynn and Arturo Giráldez, "Born with a 'Silver Spoon': The Origin of World Trade in 1571", *Journal of World History* 6:2 (Fall 1995), 201–221.

Richard von Glahn, *Fountain of Fortune: Money and Monetary Policy in China, 1000–1700* (Berkeley: University of California Press, 1996), ch. 4, "Foreign Silver and China's 'Silver Century', 1550–1650", pp. 113–141.
William S. Atwell, "International Bullion Flows and the Chinese Economy circa 1530–1650", *Past & Present* 95 (May 1982), 68–90.

claims.wording: The same historians say Manila was not China's main supplier at first. Until at least the 1570s China's main source of foreign silver was Japan. Von Glahn writes that the silver reaching China from the Philippines before 1600 was less than what came from Japan, though still considerable. He adds that Chinese merchants first brought the new colony food, iron and other supplies.
claims.notes:
Quote: "From the 1530s until at least the 1570s, China's primary source of foreign silver was western Japan" (Atwell 1982, p. 68); "The quantity of silver imported into China from the Philippines during this period, though less than Japanese imports, nonetheless was considerable." claims.wording: Kevin O'Rourke and Jeffrey Williamson (2002, 2004) do not deny that silver crossed the Pacific. They argue it was not yet globalisation. For them globalisation means markets joining up, and the sign of it is prices for the same goods moving closer together across the world. They find very little of that before the nineteenth century.
claims.notes:
Quote: "Globalisation became economically meaningful only with the dawn of the nineteenth century" (p. 109); "or with 1571 and the arrival in Manila of those stately galleons from Mexico" (p. 109); "there is very little evidence of world commodity price convergence in the three centuries after Columbus" (p. 113). All O'Rourke and Williamson 2004. Challenged by Flynn and Giráldez 2004, p. 87: "silver prices did in fact converge worldwide, not once but twice". De Vries 2010, p. 719, note 34: "the lack of substantial and lasting convergence between European and Asian silver prices".
